> However, before I Decree the Suit, in my view, it is necessary to state that, in my view it is time that Courts take note of the reality existing today, unfortunately litigation takes an inordinately long time. METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
8b60ee8c5868e308a03af11c66851f6aadc624bd:
The law being what is set out hereinabove, the true owners who are entitled to the properties, and who should by all rights get back the properties, are though no fault of their deprived of their property during the period that it takes for cases to be decided. c5e53aa1ea615931d62abbb8ac29da9c76025f65:
However, this would not be so in cases of big Corporations and/or Public Bodies who have no financial constraints; who have proper legal advice and who enter into Agreements knowing fully well what the purpose of the Agreement is. 6a4cc66f62a5535e041a09577d7779e94546d8a3:

> 7. We have heard learned Counsel for both the parties and have perused the record thoroughly. There can be no manner of. doubt that cite11†Section 6 of the Act provides for a summary remedy to any person dispossessed without consent, otherwise than in due course of law and such person is entitled to recover possession by filing a suit before the expiry of six months from the elate of dispossession. e1b321efd6e956636a749187f00ebe57503a23c3:
If the plaintiff disputes any agreement between the parties or raises a dispute that he was a lessee under the terms of the agreement then the Court will find out the intention of the parties and which would be a question of fact depending upon the various factors and circumstances of the case.

b3faced956932b84ab0e99c67d755b1e7ac8e30a:
However, so far as the present case is concerned it is an admitted case of the plaintiff that the agreement dated 27th December, 1974 was an agreement of leave and licence and in the plaint also it came with a definite case of licensee and not lessee. afacc99e990594506ea3d11dfa57ab0860b93499:
It is also an admitted position in the case that the period of licence though had come to an end on 31st December, 1986 but the company never took law into its own hands much less used any force in order to dispossess the bank from the premises. b9f45c24719dafff54d2d95759bc603b3126c77d:

3f53cf0485af8a1a547c65544b6cea9f2e3749b4:

c9fc25409fc23976aac55dcd53bf2177fe5dcbdd:
We have no hesitation in holding that the purpose behind cite11†Section 6 of the Act is to restrain a person from using force and to dispossess a person without his consent otherwise than in due course of law. In the present case in our view the plaintiff has not been dispossessed by using any force. Admittedly the bank is a licensee and the period of such licence came to an end on 31st December, 1986 and thereafter its possession was that of a trespasser.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
84f7e341dee90c553377f8af8eba2936c905bdfe:
On account of fire having broken out on 12th April, 1990 the bank had to stop its business and in fact it has started its business at some other place. In case the intention of the company would have been to dispossess the bank by force, it could have done so soon after the expiry of the period of licence, but admittedly nothing was done for more than three years till the fire broke out on 12th April, 1990.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
5bac4c11e4a75770f67e31985f1b1a88261c21db:
The question now is whether the plaintiff bank who is admittedly a licensee and having become a trespasser after 31st December, 1986 could claim recovery of possession against the owner.

2d15e6536f2b18f1601eb6e337eef9352a56a70c:
> 9. The only prohibition under the provisions of cite11†Section 6 of the Act is not to use force and not to use any unlawful means for dispossessing a person. The ratio of the decided cases is that the Court in trying a suit under cite11†Section 6 of the Act will not go into the question of title. There cannot be any dispute with this settled proposition.

6e2e92d6aeef9ef14f628b8688096d9aaf338d44:
However, in the present case the title of the company as well as the position of the plaintiff bank that its possession was as a licensee is an admitted case.

8a6f89747844cb5e026351968fb4be20dfeec164:
> 10. Our answer in these circumstances is that the plaintiff being a licensee and having become a trespasser after 31st December, 1986 has no right to claim possession from the company who is admittedly the owner of the premises.

58a9cb1054ca695a5bb93fc526629a6d26f47b92:
> 11. Even otherwise to grant or not to grant relief under the cite12†Specific Relief Act lies in the judicial discretion of the Court. f14758d2a04b794207122c97cbad84a882b4a0e7:
> 12. If we look the matter from another angle, the High Court itself has made the observations that it was most unfortunate that big corporations and public bodies (the syndicate bank here) who should be setting example to others, are taking advantage of delays of litigation and not abiding by their commitments, entered into with full knowledge of what the commitments were.

1f86afed92f2a11d572906e65fcc89b325b88781:
Not only that the High Court indirectly suggested the defendant company to file a suit for possession based on title and in the view of the High Court this was the course which the defendants must adopt. The High Court further observed that while relief cannot be denied to the plaintiffs, some opportunity must be given to the defendants to obtain such orders as they may be advised to protect their rights in the property.

2b723a3ece3493c73de3cd4cca42f527c4344914:
We are told that after the decision of the High Court the company has already filed a suit for permanent injunction on the basis of title restraining the bank from obtaining possession and an application for temporary injunction has also been filed for an interim relief.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
da2a64217e47b069dc94d6a4ca2e86c098738abc:
That being the position the result of granting any decree in this litigation under cite11†Section 6 of the Act would not serve the ends of justice and at the same time it would unnecessarily prolong litigation between the parties which would be a waste of public money as well as the valuable time of the Courts. b4cddcb8ea1e9575c46c744b11b733aa222aae7d:
> 13. The cases cited at the Bar do not deal with the situation and circumstances as arising in the case in hand before us. Those cases deal with tenants holding over after the expiry of the term of lease and such possession after holding over is entirely different from the case of a licensee remaining in occupation after the expiry of the term of licence.

The position of such licensee is no better than a trespasser and if the true owner comes into possession of the premises without using any force or on account of fire or other act of vis major, in my view it would not be in the interest of justice to grant a decree for possession in favour of such licensee under cite11†Section 6 of the Act.

> 14. The criminal cases dealing with the question of right of private defence allowed to a trespasser dispossessed by force will not lend any assistance in deciding the present case.

38bb87480689e5995a759995deff2f168705dd16:
> 15. In cite13†Lallu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh and Ors. this Court cited with approval the following observations made by Chagla, C.J. in K. K. Verma v. Naraindas C, Malkani.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
ae8a193dfbf840cd51d5c8906016c7a68ebda8c7:
Under the Indian law the possession of a tenant who has ceased to be a tenant is protected by law. Although he may not have a right to continue in possession after the termination of the tenancy his possession is judicial and that possession is protected by statute.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
60c60a63877eb4aec83fac0b2678cc01dd60283d:
Under cite14†Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act a tenant who has ceased to be a tenant may sue for possession against his landlord if the landlord deprives him of possession otherwise than in due course of law, but a trespasser who has been thrown out of possession cannot go to Court under cite14†Section 9 and claim possession against the true owner.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
9abc2da46683e9612e35abf1dcdd580e3fe308ad:
In the above passage it has been clearly observed that a trespasser who has been thrown out of possession cannot go to Court under cite14†Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act (now cite11†Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963) and claim possession against the true owner.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
e77191a54fa77ad1104c51038d536dabaa1ed6bd:
16. Another case, very near to the facts of the case in hand, decided by a Bench of three Judges of this Court is cite15†D.H, Maniar and Ors. v. Wanian Laxman Kudav . It was held cite15†in cite15†the above case that a person continuing in possession of the premises after termination, withdrawal or revocation of the licence continues to occupy it as a trespasser or as a person who has no semblance of any right to continue in occupation of the premises. Such a person cannot be called a licensee at all.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
c61d80eb43ac5e478792f922710d39eed9449f52:
17. Thus in my view the plaintiff bank in the facts and circumstances of the present case is not entitled to any decree under cite11†Section 6 of the Act. In the result I allow this appeal, set aside the judgment of the High Court dated 6th November, 1990 and dismiss the suit. In the facts and circumstances of the case parties shall bear their own costs.

18. Statute law would change the course of justice over night. But the judiciary, lay brick by brick, precedents, to march forward as an instrument of rule of law, for smooth social order. Modus operandi adopted, to get into possession, in other words, to dispossess the person in occupation should not camouflage the consequences that would flow from the action.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}

The resultant effect must be considered in their proper perspectives and the law should be put on rails preventing deflection of the course of justice, in particular under cite16†Article 141 of the Constitution. Lest the people lose faith in the efficacy of the rule of law.

d8e3c0c161265b7eaa0ad033010cbf56f80d0d31:
The conduct of the litigant, be it a corporate personality or an ordinary citizen whether would be relevant to diffuse the effect of law made me to have anxious reflections on the questions raised reminding myself that perceptual or attitudinal slant, however small it may appears to be, would give birth to immense consequences. This made me, despite my profound and personal respect to my learned brother, with all humility at my command to express my inability to agree with his proposed draft judgment.

The appellant, the owner of the Hotel Oberoi Towers, situated at Nariman Point, Bombay, negotiated with the respondent and took a loan for its construction.

22a8ae2dc64816b4ea113396f839050462e35562:
The respondent shall keep the interior of the licensed premises in good state of repairs with liberty to the appellant to inspect the same from time to time and. to ensure that the premises are always kept in a first class condition and furnished with elegant furniture. The rest of the covenants are omitted being irrelevant.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
fd456c51ce0ca8b92b9d3c5caff5be57ff652346:
20. The appellant by notices dated September 17-18, 1984 and April, 1986 requested the respondent to Vacate the demised premises by December 27, 1986 who in turn requested by letter dated July 8, 1986 to renew the licence for a further period of 12 years. On August 9, 1986 the appellant informed the respondent that they are not agreeable for renewal. On January 22, 1990 the appellant gave notice to the respondent to vacate the premises but the respondent did not vacate.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
028bfed60900479a29e3bd38a7c3a4fb3c110e42:
On April 12, 1990 fire broke out in the Oberoi Hotel and a part of the demised premises was also disfigured due to splashing of water and smoke of carbons. Consequently, in terms of the Fire Brigade direction and at the request of the appellant, the respondent had to vacate a portion of the building on the ground floor and shifted his part of the business elsewhere and the appellant had undertaken to renovate it and redeliver the property.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
7dd1a2ca71a568bfb971adf8b18c167b7dc05930:
The respondent kept the furniture and other items in a portion of the demised premises. The duplicate key which was with the respondent was handed over, on request, to the appellant. As per Annexure 'R' dated June 15, 1990, the respondent claimed that the appellant had promised to hand-over the premises to the respondent within three or four months on carrying out the repairs and renovation work. Despite the respondent's asking the appellant to hand over possession to it, the appellant did not do the same.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
26a3b5de21d49f44794452f9776274b5e676df76:
On the other hand by a letter dated June 19, 1990, the appellant asked the respondent to remove all its belongings which necessitated the respondent to lay suit No.2735 of 1990 for possession, on the Original Side of the High Court at Bombay on August 29, 1990, under cite11†Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act 47 of 1963 for short 'the Act' and took out notice of motion on August 29, 1990 for appointment of a receiver and injunction.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
b9fce0d5e80e39c8f666d475df5cd803bc79d790:
In terms of the undertaking given by the appellant the Court passed an order on August 30, 1990 which was upheld in Appeal No.961 of 1990 dated September 12, 1990. While the Receiver petition was being argued, Shri Nadman made "with prejudice offer" that he was prepared to treat the hearing as a trial of the suit and that the affidavits, evidence and documents would be the base to decide the suit.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
e25a7360af5f9aff3d3ddb81d4efed99f6fccd85:
It was also stated as narrated in the High Court judgment, that "defendants are willing to proceed on the footing that the plaintiff had been dispossessed as alleged in the plaint"..... The defendants are proceeding on the basis that the plaintiff has been dispossessed as alleged. The defendants are not pressing their case that the plaintiff had earlier expressed an intention to vacate and that it had voluntarily vacated in pursuance of that intention".
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
3b83452f0d7ebe427f5a4e1f07ce934cd771ac48:
On this understanding two issues were raised and the case was argued. The High Court by judgment dated November 6, 1990 held that for the purpose of the suit it is admitted that the plaintiff was dispossessed on July 19, 1990. The suit was filed within a period of six months from the date of dispossession. The respondent could not have been dispossessed except by due process of law. After the expiry of licence they have animus possidendi.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
2c6c0d6de3e59b2c1396c51b1f486b3842841e38:
The moment the licence was terminated their possession was that of a trespasser but it was a settled possession. The appellant cannot be allowed to take the law into its hands. They must acquire possession only through a court of law. Therefore, the suit is maintainable. Accordingly, the High Court granted a decree directing the appellant to hand over possession of the suit premises, to the respondent. However, its implementation was stayed for a period of 10 weeks from that day.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
0a6041af77d5e608dd427392b32c1b286791bf09:
Thereafter, the appellant laid the suit No.4000 of 1990 in December, 1990 and also the Special Leave Petition.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
e6738851635055db69c86ce511730373c22d6a7d:
21. Shri Nariman, learned Senior Counsel contended that cite11†Section 6 of the Act would be applicable only if a person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law. The appellant had not dispossessed the respondent; on the other hand the respondent, due to vis major, had handed over possession to the appellant and repossession asked for was refused. In this factual backdrop, cite11†Section 6 is not attracted.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
937df51f1d78237f1ad3542bf4b7ac49d862767b:
Even otherwise it was contended that admittedly fire broke out on April 12, 1990 in the Oberoi Hotel. The respondent had handed over possession of the premises. They admitted in their letter dated May 26, 1990 that they had vacated the premises on April 12, 1990 and requested ,to redeliver possession of the premises to the respondents. These facts clearly establish that the respondent had voluntarily vacated the premises and was not dispossessed.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
4ba601af3a33a87e4872b6764956019c5f7da9d5:
Even otherwise the possession of the Bank must be juridical possession and the Bank must be illegally dispossessed and then only the suit under cite11†Section 6 would lie. The appellants committed no illegality in taking possession of the demised premises. Alternatively it was contended that after expiry of the period of licence on December 12, 1986, the respondent is a trespasser, and a trespasser thrown out of possession cannot claim pos-session under cite11†Section 6 against the true owner.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
0a5f0103a2344d7bf79918c6effb88ce4cfbc3dc:
Even on that premise also the decree for possession is illegal. The High Court having found that the respondent had vacated the premises due to fire having been broken, went wrong in holding that the suit is maintainable.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
0d9cf0ec98e347daa9cdeb4a87fd32d95a84e8de:
22. Shri Ganesh, learned Counsel for the respondent contended that as Shri Nariman conceded in the High Court that the respondent had been dispossessed from the suit premises, it is no longer open to the appellant to contend that the respondent has not been dispossessed. This Court has to proceed on the finding recorded by the High Court that the respondent had been dispossessed and from that date the suit was admittedly filed within 6 months. The respondent claimed renewal in terms of the contract.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
6d661e763bb38be16650c51947e8412d1b7a38a6:
The possession of the respondent is not that of a trespasser but is a legal, juridical or settled possession. Possession was not obtained in due course of law and that, therefore, the decree for possession is legal. The right of appeal and a review of decree under cite11†Section 6 are expressly barred. Therefore, this Court while exercising its plenary power under cite17†Article 136 would not review the decree of the High Court.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
661b4e11c9b177d33ffd1c98e56bcf729966c4e4:
23. The first question that emerges is whether the respondent had been dispossessed except in due course of law. cite11†Section 6 of the Act reads thus:
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
6cfadd659cdeb7963899d5d0d4cb0ead90f66082:
> 6(1) If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person claiming through him may, by suit, recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
91dc217296b474b619c934c5b91f3ae11161db10:
> (2) No suit under this section shall be brought:
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
0ad57b3472dd3d176ac9b9303355c819fc0ea056:
> (a) after the expiry of six months from the date of dispossession; or
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
ef6555299d79dda3f65df6ecd81312a16c9c167a:
> (3) No appeal shall lie from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section, nor shall any review of any such order or decree be allowed.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
015bb806f79d00c2b0705852e92d262abad912b5:
> (4) Nothing in this section shall bar any person from suing to establish his title to such properly and to recovery possession thereof.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
b5e8446f38c39fc2e562b1339e4b5622c33ebd4f:
24. A reading thereof manifests the legislative intent that if any person is dispossessed from immovable property without his consent otherwise than in due course of law, the person dispossessed or any person claiming through him, is empowered to lay the suit to recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such a suit. But it shall be laid before expiry of six months from the date of dispossession. Such suit shall not lie against the Government.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
f6a04ba3206d0671fb74e9fb01aaee446fde8fff:
The decree or any order passed in that suit shall not be subject to any appeal or review. But it is no bar to any person to sue to establish his title to such property and to recover possession thereof under cite18†Section 5 , in the manner provided in cite19†the CPC , 1908. The question, therefore, is whether the respondent has been dispossessed without his consent.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
e90422373daefdc33ec75c95551c531a0375d0c2:
It is clear that the respondent had handed over a part of the premises, to the appellant, due to vis major occurred on April 12, 1990 in the hotel and pursuant to a request made by the appellant that too to comply with the conditions laid by Fire Brigade. It was asserted by the respondent that the appellant had promised to re-deliver possession. It also claimed that it had a right to renewal under the contract. Since civil suit is pending, it is not necessary to consider whether it is a lease or licence.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
380cc4356926bc1daa3594ae5da9a9a26894ddc2:
Suffice to proceed as pleaded that it is a licence. Sri Nariman conceded in the High Court as extracted hereinbefore, that without prejudice to their right and for the purpose of the suit, the respondent was dispossessed in the manner spoken to in the plaint. The High Court also proceeded on this footing. The counsel for the respondent therein, though objected to and insisted upon the trial of the suit, he agreed to argue, due to the concession made by the counsel for the appellant.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
3821dbe279e6cf1d4e703e20c12ffea6d9a9389b:
In fairness to Shri Nariman, he reiterated before us that he made the concession as extracted by the High Court. In my considered view, it is not open to the appellant to contend now that the respondent had not been dispossessed from the suit premises.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
3b306007794c31295094b717b07acba45d974974:
As stated in the pleadings and is clear from the documents filed in support thereof that the respondent claimed that it delivered possession to the appellants only to effect renovation and refurnishing of the suit premises with an undertaking to redeliver possession. They retained animus possedendie. It is clear from the fact that part of the furniture is still in part of the demised premises. It must be concluded that they have been dispossessed without their consent.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
c7c233d5c3670e8c27d22931b895f9ad46c22373:
25. The crucial question is whether the respondent is entitled to recover possession under cite11†Section 6 of the Act. Shri Nariman contended that the appellant had terminated the licence by a notice and thereafter the possession of the Bank is that of a trespasser. At no point of time, after determination of the licence, the appellant acquiesced to the possession of the respondent. Therefore, its possession is not juridical.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
6d3bd9e6daea0bcbad7d1ce2f2bc760647d376ef:
Unless the respondent remains and continues to remain in juridical and settled possession, the discretion under cite11†Section 6 would not he exercised in favour of such trespasser, in particular, as against the true owner. Respondent being an instrumentality of the state as a model person should not retain possession after the expiry of the period of licence.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
07b899fb6babb82eab1cace944dc98f1d93be019:
The judicial discretion given to the court under cite11†Section 6 must be exercised only in favour of the person in lawful possession on date of dispossession with proven right to retain possession as on the date of the suit. The respondent lost its right to specific performance of the contract of renewal in 1989, since the appellant had expressly refused in 1986 to renew licence. The respondent had no enforceable remedy for possession and it continued to remain a trespasser.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
0186c8319be92f0b355a616e1389b3d31f0c8b94:
26. In support thereof he placed strong reliance on Amirudin v. Mohamad Jamal I.L.R. (15) Bombay 685; cite13†Lallu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh and Ors. ; cite20†Yar Muhammad and Anr. v. Lakshmi Das and Ors. ; cite21†Maganlal Radia v. State of Maharashtra 1970 (72) Bombay Law Reporter 734; cite15†D.H. Maniar and Ors. v. Waman Laxman Kudav ; cite22†Puran Singh Sahni v. Smt. Sundari Shagwandas Kriplani and Ors. ; Brigadier K.K. Verma and Anr. v. Naraindas C.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
17ed015c3ad89510ea1ec04e3a830319077e8737:
Malkhani ILR 1954 Bombay 950; cite23†Neyveli Lignite Corpn. Ltd. and Ors. v. K.S. Narayana lyer ; cite24†Chandu Lal v. Municipal Corpn. of Delhi ; and cite25†Harshadkumar Sundarlal Dalal and Ors. v. Hasmukhben and Ors. 1983 (1) Gujarat Law Reporter 383.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
2d27dbcb61f12f2676d00ddc5fbda503205bde37:
27. The contention of Sri Nariman that dispossession by any means, fair or foul unless it is visited with breach of peace and is not amenable to exercise of power under cite11†Section 6 , would be fraught with insidious and pernicious effects on the efficacy of the rule of law as it germinates, generates or inculcates disbelief and apathy therein and drives the people to extra legal remedies.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
5baf4cbbde57cf56de45da6b52c29e3aa1a7501a:
In my considered view, therefore, that possession obtained either by violence, misrepresentation, fraud, coercion, undue influence, seemingly innocuous but hidden with oblique motive or any other mode or method unlawful or otherwise except in due course of law attracts cite11†Section 6 . Law frowns upon such conduct. The court accords legitimacy and legality only to possession taken in due course of law.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
b66796ae7a1455f410a6efc3f74d89411f62ba10:
In cite11†Section 6 proceedings the consideration of the right, title or interest in immovable property either of the person claiming possession as an owner or under colour of title or person dispossessed or threatened to be dispossessed are irrelevant. It concerns itself whether the person was dispossessed without his consent and in due course of law and whether the suit was laid within six months from the date of the suit.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
0b9f1f158abd5cdb72952520f9d5856a02425b76:
The claim based on title or possessing title, after six months, would be gone into in a suit under cite18†Section 5 of the Act. Therein all relevant considerations would enter into the area of consideration.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
b986bd29627a5f496501c16f0a6f2e050aa24455:
28. cite26†Section 52 of the Indian Easements Act defines licence thus:
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
635fda77a989a58b6108347c2ab3734738887c42:
> Where one person grants to another, or to a definite number of other persons, a right to do, or continue to do, in or upon the immovable property of the grantor something which would, in the absence of such right, be unlawful, and such right does not amount to an easement or an interest in the property, the right is called a license.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
37f7d81d4e66dc58dd952ee125c6374fae88e245:
29. It would be apparent from the definition that the permission by one person to another or a body of persons to do or continue to do upon an immovable property of the grantor is an authority or power to do one or series of acts, without which it is illegal or unlawful. The legal possession is always with the licensor and it does not create any interest or an estate in the licensee. A licensee is a person, who is neither a servant nor a "rank trespasser", but had come into possession with an authority.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
3f895a603af9854ddc2db5f5cc2b6b9840c7bc1e:
A rank trespasser is one who does not stand in any contractual relationship with the owner of the premises, A trespasser is also one who lawfully enters into but unlawfully remains in possession of the property without the consent or acquiescence of the owner.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
472c06d75123a6792dadb4fae57aa899256edf37:
If one goes into possession of the property of another with invitation or permission for instance to a shop or cinema theater, or marriage hall to celebrate a marriage his initial entry is lawful but if he refuses to leave that place and unlawfully squats on it, he becomes a trespasser of a transient origin with no vestige of right. The initial entry into possession is obviously for short duration with a specified purpose.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
c2d58b004c4bc736ebd7adeb4f625eee9e0c2612:
But if he enters upon the land under a contract and uses the land or premises and docs continuous business therein for well over a long period peacefully and uninterruptedly and continues to do the same even after the expiry or termination of licence, the important question arises whether he is a rank trespasser without any protection of law.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
762016b890b6073817f38f552c61d789091c0dbc:
30. In cite27†Midnapur Zamindary Co. Ltd. v, Naresh Narayan Roy and Ors. 51 Indian Appeals 293 (P.C.), the Privy Council held that in India persons are not permitted to take forcible possession. They must obtain such possession as they are entitled to by proper course. In our jurisprudence governed by rule of law even an unauthorized occupant can be ejected only in the manner provided by law.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
5130bd549a7cd9f93df5274474cee303ee8a70ed:
The remedy under cite11†Section 6 is summary and its object is to prevent self help and to discourage people to adopt any means fair or foul to dispossess a person unless dispossession was in due course of law or with consent.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
cd378b9d24e41d8697ef9522f501de0f30187908:
31. What is meant by due course of law? Due course of law in each particular case means such an exercise of the powers by duly constituted Tribunal or Court in accordance with the procedure established by law under such safeguards for the protection of individual rights. A course of legal proceedings according to the rules and principles which have been established in our system of jurisprudence for the enforcement and protection of private rights.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
3bfedc887f1cccd6ca9572c0eba180261f902098:
To give such proceedings any validity, there must thus be a Tribunal competent by its constitution, that is bylaw of its creation, to pass upon the subject-matter of the suit or proceeding; and, if that involves merely a determination of the personal liability of the defendant, it must be brought within its jurisdiction by service of process within the state, or his voluntary appearance.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
d62ec51b9e9206dd40e14257e31dfeaf5adc38d5:
Due course of law implies the right of the person affected thereby to be present before the Tribunal which pronounces judgment upon the question of life, liberty or property in its most comprehensive sense; to be heard, by testimony or otherwise, and to have the right of the controversy by proof, every material fact which bears on the question of fact or liability be conclusively proved or presumed against him. This is the meaning of due course of law in a comprehensive sense.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
512e423ec16223ba567d975b9e2eda9e23b5a6a3:
32. In Rudrappa v. Narsingrao (1905) I.L.R. 29 Bombay 213, a Division Bench consisting of Sir Jcnkins, Chief Justice, as he then was and Batchelor, J. held that the word "due course of law" in Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act (Old Act), as merely equivalent to the word 'legally' is, we think, to deprive them of a force and a significance which they carry on their very face. For a thing, which in perfectly legal, may still be by no means a thing done 'in due course of law'.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
fbe3e932048c8a9e8efacf422e2231415849a9a9:
To enable this phrase to be predicated of it, it is essential, speaking generally, that the thing should have been submitted to the consideration and pronouncement of the law, and the 'due course of law' means, we lake it, the regular normal process and effect of the law operating on a matter which has been laid before it for adjudication". In that case when the owner unilaterally dispossessed the tenant holding over the court upheld the decree for possession under cite14†Section 9 .
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
c81231db107fb9c0195ed802e44d76a9d7fbf86c:
The court further held that "this, in our opinion, is the primary and natural meaning of the phrase, <>in strict compliance of law though it may be applied in a derivative or secondary sense to other proceedings held under the direct authority of the law; in this sense it may be said, for instance, that revenue or taxes are collected in due course of law. A Full Bench of five Judges per majority of four in cite28†Tamizuddin v. Ashrub Ali ILR (31) Calcutta 647, Ghosh, J.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
0f30f861ef419751be19fd2ba92be6a78a9756b8:
(one of concurring Judges) held that when tenancy was not put an end to as the law requires, he remains upon the land as a tenant and necessarily if he is legal he is entitled to claim possession as a tenant. His possession is different from that of a person who enters into the land as a trespasser but if he is evicted illegally, he is entitled to put back in possession according to provision of cite14†Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act though he has no title to the land.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
b738b34ed6b85a8995e32e9a117895e3fe7edb8e:
It is to be noted that the case relates to the tenant who is entitled to remain in possession as tenant holding over after the expiry of his lease but the ratio is significant that on expiry of the lease or licence no one can take possession unilaterally except in due course of law, though the respondent had no legal title. In cite29†Jeewanmal and Ors. v. Dr.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
f8bc544791f4f9894fa706b7c71056bad9546192:
Dharamchand Khatri and Ors. , the court discountenanced the incompetent Mandi Development Officer taking over possession of the land from the petitioners. Even the modicum of procedure followed by the Board to take possession was held to be "not in regular normal process". In cite23†Neyveli Lignite Corporation 's case (supra), the respondent, a tenant holding over who was given on lease to run a canteen, on expiry of the lease, did not vacate it, though asked for.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
e935033bb19f3048f2c132b68abc6e1cb293a712:
The security officer with the assistance of the police made an inventory of the articles and kept the furniture in a room therein and had taken possession. Though he was present, the tenant did not object to taking possession but later on issued a legal notice claiming damages from the Corporation. In that case he was evicted by a summary procedure, i.e. in due course of law. So the remedy under cite11†Section 6 was not available.

Societies Act. It is also of no avail to the appellant. It, therefore, cannot be created by contract and arises only by implication of law when a person who has been in possession under a: lawful title continues in possession after that title has been determined, without the consent of the person entitled. The act of holding over after the expiration of the term does not necessarily create a tenancy of any kind. If the lessee remaining in possession after the determination of the term, the common law rule is that he is a tenant on sufferance. The expression "holding over" is used in he sense of retaining possession.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
5ca9e9780a5c1610da76049bd4badeea26507359:
A distinction should be drawn between a tenant continuing in possession after the determination of the lease, without the consent of the landlord and a tenant doing so with the landlord's consent. The former is called a tenant by sufferance in the language of the English law and the latter class of tenants is called a tenant holding over or a tenant at will. The lessee holding over with the consent of the lessor is in a better position than a mere tenant at will.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
47a8e9009ab1ce5143ed1701c3a82c727ab25059:

The assent of the landlord to the continuance of the tenancy after the determination of the tenancy would create a new tenancy. The possession of a tenant who has ceased to be a tenant is protected by law.

2cf16d25b7bda4f620e77ab32a481fbb5cd11933:
J U D G M E N T (Arising out of SLP (Civil) No. 20366/2002) ARIJIT PASAYAT,J Leave granted.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
7cc54db209851b5e5e0da2b982ba3d10ad118159:
The appellants who were plaintiffs in a suit filed before the learned Civil Judge, Senior Division, Srirampur have questioned legality of the conclusions arrived at by the Courts below holding that the plaint filed by them was to be rejected in terms of cite11†Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure , 1908 (in short the 'Code'). The plaintiffs claimed to be tenants under respondent No.2, Shaneshwar Deosthan Trust (hereinafter referred to as the 'trust').
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
302f213b557eb3de97743ab999f3f3f9ea5d142c:
Its trustees and the Assistant Charity Commissioner (in short the 'Commissioner') were the other defendants. Plaintiffs claimed that they were tenants of the trust of which the defendants Nos. 3 to 13 were the trustees. Alleging that they have been forcibly evicted notwithstanding continuance of the tenancy, the suit was filed for the following reliefs:
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
63108ca5e58670025c10fc841f1e427a433a5f25:
> A) Plaintiff no. 1 to 17, be declared as the tenants of the properties described in the plaint belonging to temple Trust, of which defendant No.2 to 13 are trustees.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
f2f8d37e359afc3038daf7449b5b0e88559a1074:
> B) Defendant No.1 to 13, be permanently restrained by an order of injunction not to evict plaintiff No.1 to 13, forcibly with the help of police and also not to interfere in their business being carried on by them in suit shops, and not to interfere in the possession of suit shops in any manner-whatsoever, either by themselves or by their servants, agents, relatives or anybody claiming through or under them.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
1e16228f5609ba6bdd9f0100901d1b5d8678f788:
> C) Direct the defendant No. 2 to 13, to pay compensation for the loss caused to the plaintiffs on account of their acts of omission and commission as described in the plaint, committed by them prior to the filing of the suit and during pendency of suit for the damage that may be caused to the plaintiffs.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
7830695b60ddea1e5992d0b0fc82ecbb3a46d976:
> D) Defendant No.1 be directed to enquire into the illegal acts, committed by defendant No.2 to 13, and issue appropriate direction to that effect.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
a8bf62127e8d12fab9f9cde041ab4d05222cb016:
The suit was numbered as R.C.S. No.160/1997 in the trial Court. The stand of the plaintiffs-appellants essentially was that the tenancy was for a period of 11 years and not for 11 months as claimed by the trust. An application was filed by the trust raising a preliminary plea that the plaint is liable to be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
1d4cdaf717784d8b23710458667e71f27f6a1073:
With reference to cite12†Section 80 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 (in short the 'Act') it was urged that no Civil court had jurisdiction to decide or deal with any question which by or under the Act is to be decided or dealt with by any officer or authority under the Act and in respect of which the decision or order of such officer or authority has been made final and conclusive. The trial Judge framed two preliminary issues, i.e.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
85989007f337d30ec1e91dcb1f5aa6d10df36ddb:
(a) whether the suit was liable to be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code for want of cause of action, and (b) whether the suit was tenable against all the defendants. Findings in respect of the preliminary issues were recorded against the plaintiffs.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
c6c2e6e517f8d2eb33cf49004342cb2aa8c2b7d4:
A finding was recorded that the plaint does not disclose any cause of action and also in view of the specific provisions of the Act, the jurisdiction vests only with the District Court to give direction to Commissioner and in any event cite12†Section 80 of the Act took away jurisdiction of the Civil Court and the plaint was rejected.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
de4d9aef69a90da3e6728e07ba9a82fe899537a6:
Challenging the judgment and decree dated 21.10.2000 passed by the learned Civil Judge, Senior Division, Srirampur, an appeal was preferred before the District Court which was numbered as Regular Civil Appeal No.178 of 2000. The appeal was dismissed and the decree passed by the trial Court was confirmed by II Additional District Judge at Srirampur, Ahmed Nagar District.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
4c43a30a5446125df0bb645575f66b77793843a7:
The matter was carried in Second Appeal before the High Court which by the impugned judgment upheld the findings recorded by the Courts below. Before the High Court, it was contended by the appellants that cite13†Sections 50 , cite14†51 and cite12†80 of the Act had no application and the lease being for 11 years, the action of the trust in dispossessing the plaintiffs forcibly cannot have the approval of law.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
6c93f8d845bbb6fdc124d46e6450cea674fc180c:
The stand of the trust was to the effect that the plaintiffs have not approached the Court with clean hands. They had tried to get relief from the High Court by filing a petition under cite15†Article 226 of the Constitution of India, 1950 (in short the 'Constitution'). They failed to comply with the interim directions given by the High Court and before the date posted before the High Court for consideration of the interim orders, they filed the suit and prayed for injunction.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
14f6187dfa8fc5d1d7ed266086db47ac0f01b61a:
Subsequently, the writ petition was withdrawn. The plaint filed by the plaintiffs did not disclose any cause of action and in any event the relief sought for could not have been granted by the Civil Court in view of the specific provisions contained in cite13†Sections 50 , cite14†51 and cite12†80 of the Act. There was no forcible dispossession as claimed. The Courts below were justified in rejecting the plaint.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
319fffda4cfd9a882ffe9b2cc582e3304490bb28:
The High Court accepted the plea of the trust and dismissed the second appeal affirming the conclusions arrived by the Courts below.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
e6c7d283a5eaef6c86f400003f8f8a963b3f270f:
In support of the appeal, Mr. V.A. Mohta, learned senior counsel appearing for the appellants submitted that the Courts below have lost sight of the nuances of Order VII Rule 11 of the Code. Even if for the sake of arguments it is conceded that some reliefs were to be dealt with by the authorities under the Act, the reliefs were severable and the Civil Court had jurisdiction to deal with them.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
292c4da6f720de1b306dc3511968b27d346637f7:
The dispute projected in the suit essentially related to the question of tenancy and the relationship between the plaintiffs and the defendant-trust vis-`-vis the question of tenancy, the term of tenancy are matters intermittently linked with these basic issues. Such issues cannot be decided by the authorities under the Act. Therefore, the rejection of the plaint under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code cannot be maintained in law.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
f6a52c439baa18aaedd24483d476e9d5afff95f0:
The plaintiffs were dispossessed illegally and a person dispossessed illegally was entitled to protection. A person without title but in 'settled' possession as against mere fugitive possession, can get back possession if forcibly dispossessed or rather if dispossessed otherwise than by due process of law.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
b76b16b8977e06e206edc16353e094999d902823:
Per contra, Mr. A.V. Savant, learned senior counsel appearing for the defendant-trust submitted that the Courts below have concurrently found it as a matter of fact that the plaint did not disclose a cause of action and the Civil Court had no jurisdiction to deal with a matter, specifically in view of what has been statutorily provided in cite12†Section 80 of the Act. With reference to the judgment of the High court it was pointed out that the plaintiffs had not approached the Court with clean hands.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
a916a2afd9b20718e1cbd50fc266d8fea8e7c40b:
They had adopted dubious methods, did not comply with the directions of the High Court for depositing the stipulated amount. By a ruse, some reliefs have been sought for in the plaint totally out of context with the main prayers which are to be dealt with in terms of cite13†Sections 50 and cite14†51 of the Act. There were no pleadings about alleged forcible dis-possession and wholly untenable plea about the period of tenancy has been rightly rejected by the Courts below.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
788fcb766283d517fd62ba429a0c67daee278a64:
Clauses (a) and (d) of Rule 11 have full application to the facts of the case. The whole purpose in filing the suit was to somehow or other remains in possession of the shops which were leased out to them for certain periods. As a result of the actions of the plaintiffs, the trust would have been put to huge financial loss. All this according to him, disentitle the appellants from any relief under cite16†Article 136 of the Constitution.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
4b8cb7578f586f83bcfbf7baf5f2ca4e0c681c7b:
Order VII Rule 11 of the Code reads as follows:
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
18e997ec7189a1c7797b67c9b1474afafacb4988:
> Order VII Rule 11: Rejection of plaint.  The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases :-
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
21558c0f4c33be28b82f3dca1d928a6a2ac50735:
> (a) where it does not disclose a cause of action;
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
eb2fd1c588da6ba22c38412f2f527dcfd40bfc06:
> (b) where the relief claimed is undervalued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the court, fails to do so;

6ba9f7d0c5fb8fa847a843ae0901f8f28bb02764:
> (c) where the relief claims is properly valued but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so;
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
6b5c70c2ca8fdbbb4315dc5a123cea25fedb3fc7:
> (d) where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law;
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
658b38d31a1cecf5d5a949c326878abe8c97e21c:
> (e) where it is not filed in duplicate;
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
087d56cee0125716c2ef9e9bba70861c884d949e:
> (f) where the plaintiff fails to comply with the provisions of rule 9.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
c01d05aaf58c489bb1c77c22d35518e2e21838c4:
Provided that the time fixed by the Court for the correction of the valuation or supplying of the requisite stamp-paper shall not be extended unless the Court, for reasons to be recorded, is satisfied that the plaintiff was prevented by any cause of an exceptional nature for correcting the valuation or supplying the requisite stamp- paper, as the case may be, within the time fixed by the Court and that refusal to extend such time would cause grave injustice to the plaintiff."
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
933c60e5161636ed6ab20d81eaf00e52e925e6bf:
In the present case the respondent-trust has relied upon clauses (a) and (d) of Rule 11.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
6a5c3a6792fd9fdcbbb757cc79ab7ccec78898e4:
Before dealing with the factual scenario, the spectrum of Order VII Rule 11 in the legal ambit needs to be noted.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
1649a9dc3b7afa81027aece85a4858626b907f5f:
In cite17†Saleem Bhai and Ors. v. State of Maharashtra and Ors. (2003 (1) SCC 557) it was held with reference to Order VII Rule 11 of the Code that the relevant facts which need to be looked into for deciding an application thereunder are the averments in the plaint. The trial Court can exercise the power at any stage of the suit - before registering the plaint or after issuing summons to the defendant at any time before the conclusion of the trial.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
d1d59e8b0292b0b278b248fb6de3034476798bb3:
For the purposes of deciding an application under clauses (a) and (d) of Order VII Rule 11 of the Code, the averments in the plaint are the germane; the pleas taken by the defendant in the written statement would be wholly irrelevant at that stage.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
ee87db325d6c06d7fabcf5c2b41d6130259c3c2f:
In cite18†I.T.C. Ltd. v. Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal and Ors. (1998 (2) SCC 70) it was held that the basic question to be decided while dealing with an application filed under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code is whether a real cause of action has been set out in the plaint or something purely illusory has been stated with a view to get out of Order VII Rule 11 of the Code.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
6764d372272b0456f0b1be82ecf14d7f59b6a3b9:
The trial Court must remember that if on a meaningful and not formal reading of the plaint it is manifestly vexatious and meritless in the sense of not disclosing a clear right to sue, it should exercise the power under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code taking care to see that the ground mentioned therein is fulfilled. If clever drafting has created the illusion of a cause of action, it has to be nipped in the bud at the first hearing by examining the party searchingly under Order X of the Code. (See cite19†T.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}

Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal and Anr. (1977 (4) SCC 467) It is trite law that not any particular plea has to be considered, and the whole plaint has to be read. As was observed by this Court in cite20†Roop Lal Sathi v. Nachhattar Singh Gill (1982 (3) SCC 487), only a part of the plaint cannot be rejected and if no cause of action is disclosed, the plaint as a whole must be rejected.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}

In Raptakos Brett & Co.Ltd. v. Ganesh Property (1998 (7) SCC 184) it was observed that the averments in the plaint as a whole have to be seen to find out whether clause
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
577419367a87877ff5bd2acb42e209de14ad3ebe:
(d) of Rule 11 of Order VII was applicable.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
2aa77f3a6c330ae5b781bf0cd468d99ba6f63880:
There cannot be any compartmentalization, dissection, segregation and inversions of the language of various paragraphs in the plaint. If such a course is adopted it would run counter to the cardinal canon of interpretation according to which a pleading has to be read as a whole to ascertain its true import. It is not permissible to cull out a sentence or a passage and to read it out of the context in isolation.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
c996a1673e875c349757d0ed8956906d7e9d5359:
Although it is the substance and not merely the form that has to be looked into, the pleading has to be construed as it stands without addition or subtraction or words or change of its apparent grammatical sense. The intention of the party concerned is to be gathered primarily from the tenor and terms of his pleadings taken as a whole. At the same time it should be borne in mind that no pedantic approach should be adopted to defeat justice on hair- splitting technicalities.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
7a8a5fa240503f257b3fbc76d2de74ca3ac9e032:
Submission of learned counsel for respondent No.2- trust was that requirement of law being reading the plaint in its totality, the appellants cannot take the plea that they would give up or relinquish some of the reliefs sought for. That would not be permissible. The plea clearly overlooks the basic distinction between statements of the facts disclosing cause of action and the reliefs sought for. The reliefs claimed do not constitute the cause of action.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
48f59e1cc0df862063a971ddeb45a7a88d6d1399:
On the contrary, they constitute the entitlement, if any, on the basis of pleaded facts. As indicated above, Order VI Rule 2 requires that pleadings shall contain and contain only a statement in a concise form of the material facts on which the party pleading relies for his claim. If the plea of Mr. Savant, learned counsel for the respondent-trust is accepted the distinction between the statement of material facts and the reliance on them for the claim shall be obliterated.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
3116881e4a98306bccaeda9eb4290e211d70a254:
What is required in law is not the piecemeal reading of the plaint but in its entirety. Whether the reliefs would be granted on the pleaded facts and the evidence adduced is totally different from the relief claimed. All the reliefs claimed may not be allowed to a party on the pleadings and the evidence adduced.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
914056f2880ce962b364b04c79e95756743704bf:
Whether part of the relief cannot be granted by the Civil Court is a different matter from saying that because of a combined claim of reliefs the jurisdiction is ousted or no cause of action is disclosed. Considering the reliefs claimed vis-a- vis the pleadings would not mean compartmentalization or segregation, in that sense. The plea raised by the respondent-trust is therefore clearly unacceptable.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}

Keeping in view the aforesaid principles the reliefs sought for in the suit as quoted supra have to be considered. The real object of Order VII Rule 11 of the Code is to keep out of courts irresponsible law suits.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
fb323178355c9f0d8be0446624e5be58f522219a:
Therefore, the Order X of the Code is a tool in the hands of the Courts by resorting to which and by searching examination of the party in case the Court is prima facie of the view that the suit is an abuse of the process of the court in the sense that it is a bogus and irresponsible litigation, the jurisdiction under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code can be exercised.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
69646636e70d8c9031144f64f2cde74b44b840cf:
As noted supra, the Order VII Rule 11 does not justify rejection of any particular portion of the plaint. Order VI Rule 16 of the Code is relevant in this regard. It deals with 'striking out pleadings'. It has three clauses permitting the Court at any stage of the proceeding to strike out or amend any matter in any pleading i.e.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
b91bbfd28eb22a8d64cdecd990ddd41a321fa187:
(a) which may be unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, or, (b) which may tend to prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial of the suit, or, (c) which is otherwise an abuse of the process of the Court.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
0eeec03cd44659768fdc4ff3e69c192ed4a23bc3:
Order VI Rule 2(1) of the Code states the basic and cardinal rule of pleadings and declares that the pleading has to state material facts and not the evidence. It mandates that every pleading shall contain, and contain only, a statement in a concise form of the material facts on which the party pleading relies for his claim or defence, as the case may be, but not the evidence by which they are to be proved.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
719328f2f8e15fad3e7164259f3026bdcb7b9662:
There is distinction between 'material facts' and 'particulars'. The words 'material facts' show that the facts necessary to formulate a complete cause of action must be stated. Omission of a single material fact leads to an incomplete cause of action and the statement or plaint becomes bad. The distinction which has been made between 'material facts' and 'particulars' was brought by Scott, L.J. in Bruce v. Odhams Press Ltd. (1936) 1 KB 697 in the following passage :
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
15a56cb2f63c06f5bfefc987fa8475c90e3989ce:
> The cardinal provision in Rule 4 is that the statement of claim must state the material facts. The word "material" means necessary for the purpose of formulating a complete cause of action; and if any one "material" statement is omitted, the statement of claim is bad; it is "demurrable" in the old phraseology, and in the new is liable to be "struck out" under R.S.C. Order XXV, Rule 4 (see Philipps v. Philipps ((1878) 4 QBD
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
f3bae3042a4b38c4205e41e69afd05dc8753a813:
> 127)); or "a further and better statement of claim" may be ordered under Rule 7.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
22e75ef8d4bcc38b184c39cd9a4470b7e50155c6:
The function of "particulars" under Rule 6 is quite different. They are not to be used in order to fill material gaps in a demurrable statement of claim - gaps which ought to have been filled by appropriate statements of the various material facts which together constitute the plaintiff's cause of action. The use of particulars is intended to meet a further and quite separate requirement of pleading, imposed in fairness and justice to the defendant.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
6a66df42fac5c95bf6c2542684d69a9e8fd1fc01:
Their function is to fill in the picture of the plaintiff's cause of action with information sufficiently detailed to put the defendant on his guard as to the case he had to meet and to enable him to prepare for trial.
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
0db0885e9f07dbf89c979034ea1b1e504d5b9ffa:
The dictum of Scott, L.J. in Bruce case (supra) has been quoted with approval by this Court in cite21†Samant N. Balkrishna v. George Fernandez (1969 (3) SCC 238), and the distinction between "material facts" and "particulars" was brought out in the following terms:
METADATA: {"document_role": "TARGET", "role": "JUDGMENT_TEXT", "stage": "SOURCE"}
738859952b4f347c378da7dde1caa6be32a522d1:
> The word 'material' shows that the facts necessary to formulate a complete cause of action must be stated. Omission of a single material fact leads to an incomplete cause of action and the statement of claim becomes bad. The function of particulars is to present as full a picture of the cause of action with such further information in detail as to make the opposite party understand the case he will have to meet.

9c88bce8dc1594bb3bf34626c1ea1cda3de287aa:

Instead, the word 'shall' is used clearly implying thereby that it casts a duty on the Court to perform its obligations in rejecting the plaint when the same is hit by any of the infirmities provided in the four clauses of Rule 11, even without intervention of the defendant. Taking up the first aspect, it is true that where a person is in settled possession of property, even on the assumption that he has no right to remain in property, he cannot be disposed by the owner except by recourse of law. This principle is cite21†laid down in cite22†Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.

Order VII Rule 11(a)/(d) is a plaint-focused screening procedure. The court reads the whole plaint meaningfully, considers its material factual averments rather than the defendant's denials, and does not equate a prayer for relief with the facts constituting a cause of action. A Rule 11(a)/(d) challenge must be screened on the material factual allegations of the plaint as a whole, not by proving or disproving those allegations through the defence or by treating each requested relief as a separate cause of action.

A materially pleaded controversy over whether a trust's tenant relationship continued and how long the tenancy lasted is a civil tenancy subject, distinct from administering or investigating the trust under Sections 50 and 51 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act. The plaintiff's failure to establish title and the defendant's objection concerning the absence of declaratory relief do not automatically defeat an otherwise supportable possessory injunction claim. The Supreme Court rejected the defendant's proposed automatic dismissal while distinguishing the discretionary treatment of temporary injunctions.
METADATA: {"bindings": [{"entity": "E1", "role": "subject"}, {"entity": "E2", "role": "opponent"}, {"entity": "E3", "role": "property"}], "limitations": ["The conclusion concerns automatic dismissal based on title non-proof or the alleged omission of declaratory relief.", "The independent possessory basis remains necessary.", "The Supreme Court's approval of the position discussed in Kallappa Rama Londa does not establish an unconditional rule for all injunction-only suits.", "The cited Allahabad decision was distinguished as involving discretionary temporary or ad-interim relief.", "The Bombay decision was discussed as authority concerning lawful possession and threatened invasion, not as independent evidence of this case's facts.", "The complete pleadings were not supplied for independent verification.", "The defendant's rejected arguments remain attributed party claims.", "No universal procedural rule governing all disputed-title litigation is reconstructed.", "Ownership and precise boundary demarcation remain outside this conclusion."], "stage": "SUPREME_COURT_MERITS_APPEAL", "state": "TRUE", "statement_status": "LEGAL_RULE", "time_scope": "Supreme Court merits adjudication"}
649682847ed124071d3d7563f237713c4f33d6b0:
The possessory ground for protecting the plaintiff's settled possession does not itself confirm ownership in the plaintiff or conclusively reject the defendant's possible proprietary claim. The Supreme Court distinguished protection of possession from adjudication of title and expressly preserved that distinction in this case.
METADATA: {"bindings": [{"entity": "E1", "role": "subject"}, {"entity": "E2", "role": "opponent"}, {"entity": "E3", "role": "property"}], "limitations": ["This is a non-entailment proposition: protection of possession alone neither proves nor disproves ownership.", "The jurisprudential formulation is quoted by the Supreme Court from Salmond and related by that Court to Indian law.", "The source work has not been independently consulted.", "Possession may have evidential significance regarding title, but that significance is not a conclusive ownership declaration.", "The actual reservation of title is independently recorded in F11, F12 and F13.", "No proprietary or boundary determination is derived from the injunction.", "The rule does not preclude a properly constituted proprietary action."], "stage": "SUPREME_COURT_MERITS_APPEAL", "state": "TRUE", "statement_status": "LEGAL_RULE", "time_scope": "Supreme Court merits adjudication"}
d3f87bc2e9859006ba0749201cbeb979e3a29969:
Because the possessory adjudication did not resolve ownership and the Supreme Court expressly reserved title, the parties remain free to litigate their claimed titles in duly constituted proceedings. The defendant may pursue title-based recovery, but eviction is conditional on establishing a better right to possess the disputed property.
METADATA: {"bindings": [{"entity": "E1", "role": "subject"}, {"entity": "E2", "role": "opponent"}, {"entity": "E3", "role": "property"}], "limitations": ["The availability of a separate proceeding is not a present adjudication of superior title.", "The defendant's possible entitlement to eviction is expressly conditional on establishing a better right to possession.", "Neither party is guaranteed success in a subsequent proprietary action.", "No actual later filing, judgment, decree or eviction is established.", "The defendant's prior failure to prove title cannot be transformed into a definitive finding that no title exists.", "The plaintiff's protected possession does not immunize him against lawful recovery.", "The unresolved identification and boundary issues remain relevant to any future proprietary claim.", "No additional procedural admissibility, limitation or evidentiary standards are inferred.", "This application concerns the specifically reserved title question, not a general entitlement to reopen final proprietary judgments.", "The final appellate disposition is not an antecedent premise."], "stage": "SUPREME_COURT_MERITS_APPEAL", "state": "TRUE", "statement_status": "LEGAL_RULE", "time_scope": "Prospective proceedings following the possessory adjudication; no later filing established"}
d6308526e4141ad1dbfa569d69bb1c68a7a6e46c:
The Supreme Court distinguished the Allahabad decision relied on by the appellant because that decision concerned discretionary temporary or ad-interim injunctive relief in its own circumstances, whereas the present dispute concerned the merits of possession-based protection.
METADATA: {"bindings": [], "limitations": ["This represents the target court's characterization of the cited decision.", "The cited decision has not been independently examined.", "The reasoning must not be generalized to eliminate discretionary considerations at the interim-relief stage.", "No factual findings from the cited litigation are imported into the present case.", "The distinction qualifies the treatment of the defendant's procedural objection."], "stage": "SUPREME_COURT_MERITS_APPEAL", "state": "TRUE", "statement_status": "TARGET_COURT_FINDING", "time_scope": "Supreme Court merits adjudication"}
080397d5411cd652f4a16a45a62f3369c0ac5e90:
The Supreme Court dismissed the defendant's appeal. This is recorded solely as the final disposition and is not used to establish possession, title non-proof, interference, the availability of a possessory injunction basis or any other antecedent proposition.

R.C. Lahoti, B.N. Srikrishna & G.P. Mathur
